battle.title: Sorting Showdown
battle.description: Bubble, selection and the stable sort: predict each pass and pick the right sorter.

questions.text: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?
options: Elements that compare equal keep their original relative order
It always runs in O(n) time
questions.answer: Elements that compare equal keep their original relative order
questions.explanation: Stability matters when sorting records by one key after another, for example by name then by score. It says nothing about running time or memory.
One bubble pass swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs, carrying the largest value 4 to the end, but the rest is only partly fixed. Expecting a fully sorted array needs n - 1 passes.

Selection sort fixes one position per pass. Pass 0 swaps the minimum 1 into place giving [1, 2, 4, 5, 3], and pass 1 finds 2 already in place. Only two positions are fixed, so it is not fully sorted yet.

questions.text: You must sort 5 million integers held in memory as fast as reliably possible. What do you use?
options: Bubble sort, because it is the simplest
Insertion sort, because it is stable
Selection sort, because it makes the fewest swaps
A built-in O(n log n) sort such as Arrays.sort
questions.answer: A built-in O(n log n) sort such as Arrays.sort
questions.explanation: O(n log n) sorts stay practical at millions of items, while bubble, insertion and selection sort are O(n^2) and would take far too long. Fewer swaps or stability do not rescue a quadratic algorithm.

Arrays.sort on objects is stable, so words of equal length keep their input order: a before d, and bb before cc. An unstable sort could swap equal-length words, which is what the tempting options show.

coding.title: Bubble Sort Swap Counter
coding.description: Sort the array using bubble sort: repeatedly pass over the array swapping adjacent elements when the left one is strictly greater than the right one. Print the total number of swaps performed on the first line and the sorted array on the second line.
coding.outputDescription: Line 1: the swap count. Line 2: the sorted values separated by spaces.

debug.title: The Sloppy Selection
debug.description: This selection sort should print the array in ascending order, but some inputs come out only partly sorted. Input: n, then n integers. Output: the sorted integers separated by spaces.
hints: Try the input 3 1 2. What order does it print?
Already sorted input works. Look at how the inner loop picks the minimum index.
The inner loop should find the smallest remaining value, but what is each a[j] being compared against?
Compare against the current minimum, a[j] < a[min], not against a[i].
